title: Five pillars, one house
hookLine: the pillars hold up a life the way the prayer hall's columns hold the roof
carry: islam is built on five, under one roof

cards: A prayer hall has a carpet, light from the windows, a niche that points toward Mecca. And it has columns. They stand row after row, doing their one job, and the roof stays up.
A column is easy to overlook until it's missing. That's the picture behind a report the Prophet's companions passed on, one that turns religion into architecture. You met it back on day nine.
Today, the five pillars, and the house they hold up.

teach.b: Abdullah ibn Umar relates, in Sahih Muslim, that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said: Islam is built upon five. Testifying that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is His messenger. Establishing the prayer.
Giving zakat. Fasting Ramadan. And the Hajj.
Notice the verb. Not ruled by five, not summed up in five. Built.
Islam is described as a building. Second, how carefully it was kept. In the same collection, a man repeats the list back to Ibn Umar and puts the Hajj before the fast.
Ibn Umar stops him: no, fasting Ramadan and then the Hajj; that is how I heard it from the Messenger of God. A small correction, and it shows how closely he held to the exact words. Third, look back.
This block walked through the building one pillar at a time. The testimony, two sentences. The prayer, its times and its stillness.
Zakat, the share that purifies. The fast, its shield and its two joys.

And these last weeks, the pilgrimage: the boundary and the two white cloths, Arafah and Muzdalifah, the stones, the sacrifice, the haircut, the circlings, the farewell, Medina, and the longing of those who stay home.
Fourth, why one house and not five separate rules.
The pillars hold the same roof, and they bend to the person under it. Zakat falls on those with wealth, the fast has its exemptions, the Hajj is due only on those who are able.
The building is drawn to fit the people who live in it.
One house, five columns, and a roof over a whole life.

how: Muslims learn the five pillars, the testimony, prayer, zakat, the fast of Ramadan and the Hajj, from the report of Ibn Umar, and some teachers present them as the supports of one building.

o: five daily prayers, each one at its own time
the columns that hold up the roof of a mosque
the five acts Islam is built on, testimony to Hajj

games.q: you're with Ibn Umar. a man repeats the report back and puts the Hajj before the fast of Ramadan. what does Ibn Umar do?
o: lets it pass; the meaning's the same.
corrects him: fasting Ramadan, then the Hajj, as he heard it.
games.why: in Sahih Muslim he says no, fasting Ramadan and the Hajj, that is how I heard it from the Messenger of God.

practice: Go through the pillars slowly, the way you'd walk past columns in a hall: the testimony, the prayer, giving, the fast, the pilgrimage or the longing for it, and rest your attention on the one you're strongest in.
If you're learning about Islam rather than practicing it, ask which of your own daily supports is steadiest; if you pray, thank God for what's holding. The weak one can wait for tomorrow.

wordCard.voice: Five pillars. The testimony, the prayer, zakat, the fast of Ramadan and the Hajj: in Ibn Umar's report, the five Islam is built upon. Today's word.
